Bonjour and welcome to the Cyclingnews live coverage of stage 5 of the Tour de France Femmes.

As for every stage, we will have the best, most detailed, updates from the stage.

We kick-off our live coverage before each stage and add reaction and analysis after the finish.

Stage 5 sees the Tour head south into the Beaujolais region for a gruelling up-and-down from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais.

Eight classified climbs and several uncategorised ascents fill a 140km day that will be broadcast from start to finish. It all adds up to 2,900 metres of elevation gain - the second-most of the whole nine-day race.

All the stage rolls through vineyards and forests, making it a possible GC day. Will Marlen Reusser (Movistar) still be in yellow at the finish?

This is our full stage preview.

The stage roll out is 40 minutes away, with the official stage start at 14:00CET.

There are again huge crowds at the Tour.

Canyon-Sram are the latest team to sign-on in Macon.

All the riders are again wearing ice-vests, with temperatures at 29C and forecast to rise to 31C during the stage.

Dem Vollering and her FDJ United-Suez team are next to sign on.

Vollering produced a superb TT on Tuesday, as some of her GC rivals struggled. It will be fascinating to see if Vollering goes on the attack today, to try to gain more time.

It's time for Marlen Reusser to show off her new yellow jersey on the sign-on.

She also has a yellow bike, helmet and sunglasses.

Marlen Reuser spoke briefly on the sign-on podium

Lets go! The goal is to keep the jersey. I think there will be big gaps today. it's an important day

Five minutes to the roll out and so the riders line-up at the start, with the jersey wearers on the front of the grid.

C'est Parti! The speaker does his usual countdown and announces 'They're off!'

The riders face a 140km stage in the hills.

Before that they have a 7.2km neutralised ride to Km 0, where the attacks will surely start.

This is the stage map. The many climbs and twisting roads has sparked comparisons with Liege-Bastogne-Liege.

I sense it could be even harder.

The tension is already high, with an early crash. Demi Vollering was caught in it but did not go down.

The pace is high on the first climb, no attacks just yet, but sone of the sprinters are suffering at the back

The fear for the stage and the eight categorised climbs has perhaps convinced some riders and teams to race cautiously.

We spoke too soon. As soon as we posted the update the first attack came.

Vallieres, Cavallar, Mavi García, Pieterse, Spratt and Wiebes tried to spark a spurge. They were soon caught but more attacks are likely near or over the top of the 9.6km Côte de Cenves climb.

Magdeleine Vallieres (EF Education-Oatly) surges again but is kept in check.

Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx) is near the front clearly trying to stay there until the intermediate sprint point, with 98km to race.

She will have to suffer for another 30km in the rolling hills.

The pace is steady but high, with 2km to climb, and so is hurting some riders. They are fighting to hold on but some have already lost contact.

A slow in the bunch has even forced some riders to stop and put a foot down.

Look at those views across the vineyards. Wow!

Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) is up front and fights for the QOM sprint atop the Côte de Cenves.

She kicks with 100m to go and nobody really challenges her.

Pieterse scores 5 more points and extends her lead in the QOM competition to 23 points.

Pieterse is covered from head to toe in red polka-dots.

A group of 20 riders have been dropped, including Monica Trinca Colonel (Liv AlUla Jayco) who is 16th on the GC.

She will have to try to fight to get back but the twisting descents are as testing as the climbs.

Niamh Fisher-Black (Lidl-Trek) launches an attack and other riders are going after her.

Niamh Fisher-Black (Lidl-Trek) has opened a 10-second lead but nobody from the peloton has jumped across to her.

She seems to be doubting about staying out front alone but other riders seem ready to attack on the 2.1km Col de la Croix de l'Orme climb.

Indeed, other surges sweep up the Kiwi rider.

Crash! Consonni goes down.

The crash happened as some teams grabbed bidons.

Consonni called out in pain.

Polka-dot Puck strikes again.

Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) kicks away to score 2 more QOM points.

Nobody else seems to be challenging her so far today.

Fortunately Consonni is back riding after the pain of her crash.

Lets hope the Italian can rejoin the peloton.

109 riders are still in the peloton, with 27 riders in the gruppetto at 2:00.

Demi Vollering's sports director Lars Boom spoke to Eurosport at the start.

We really want to race today and gain more time. We went to race hard all day.The stage is like liege-Bastogne-Liege and I think Demi won that race last year...

How hard is the racing so far?

Well Marianne Vos (Visma) has been dropped.

The riders are on the 2.7km Côte de Saint-Christophe climb.

It's no surprise that Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) sprints to the summit to score another points.

She admitted that she took the jersey almost by chance but is now racing to keep it.

The race has left the vineyards and are in the hills, with lots of Charolais bulls in the fields.

Carlotta Cipressi (Human Powered Health) has opened a gap but the peloton is chasing her, ready to set-up Wiebes for the intermediate sprint part way up the next climb.

Carlotta Cipressi (Human Powered Health) is first to the sprint point and so scores 25 points.

Lorena Wiebes takes second a few seconds later and so scores 20 points. Lotte Kopecky takes second, so taking points away from Wiebes green jersey rivals.

Wiebes now has 131 points and is dominating the green jersey compeition. However she has few chances to score more points and her biggest rivals are the GC contenders.

Cipressi is pulled back but there is a sense that more attacks will come vey soon.

The riders enjoy a fast descent with some shade but the peloton is lined out.

The stage profile and country road make it difficult for riders and teams to feed from their cars.

Instead, riders are grabbing bidons and ice from team staff along the road in designated points.

After talking 20 points in the intermediate sprint, Lorena Wiebes is dropped and will surely slip back to the gruppetto.

Everyone is very serious in the peloton today.

items.title: Eddy Merckx out riding a bike again as lengthy recovery from hip operation progresses
items.content:
Eddy Merckx's health condition is improving, Belgian media report, as the 81-year-old all-time great of the sport returned to riding a bike outdoors for the first time in months.

Merckx confirmed the news with an Instagram reel showing footage of himself and daughter Sabine out on a sunny afternoon's ride, with Merckx himself using an e-bike to amble along a bike path, likely somewhere near his home in Belgium.

The 81-year-old fell heavily in December 2024 and fractured his right hip, needing a full replacement in an operation the following day.

Merckx told newspaper after the Tour that his condition was improving, and that has continued to be the case. After a spell back on the bike on the rollers, he has now headed outdoors, too, for more rides.

"I hope I can ride a road bike outside again someday, but I shouldn't complain, because I've come a long way," he said in an interview with last week.

items.title: Pauline Ferrand-Prévot is nowhere near done, but don't underestimate Marlen Reusser in yellow – Tour de France Femmes analysis
items.content:
On a time trial day, you can't analyse the full results and consequences until every rider is finished, but you can usually get an idea of who is winning and who is losing quite early on, and stage 4 of the Tour de France Femmes was no different.

The first sign of trouble was when Pauline Ferrand-Prévot went through the first time check well down on not only the best TT riders, but plenty of her less savvy rivals in the discipline too. The answer to the long-held question of how good her TT was unfolded in front of our eyes, and the answer was - well, not very good.

The Visma-Lease a Bike leader seemed to have a relatively upright position on the bike, ostensibly down to some old injuries that made a more aero tuck uncomfortable, and combined with her small stature and lack of TT practice, that didn't make for a terribly impressive performance.

It was also a tough day for Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime), who was nowhere near the TT level she showed at World Championships and then the Giro d'Italia, really just struggling round the course. More so than the time she lost, the fact that she is clearly not feeling good is probably the biggest blow to any overall ambitions she may have had, because this compressed race really gives you no time to feel bad and then recover.

On the flip side, the rider who quite quickly showed that they were on a very good day was Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney. The Canyon-SRAM rider and Ferrand-Prévot featured in a lot of headlines pre-TT, mentioned as two GC riders who didn't have the strongest history in the discipline. Yet whilst Ferrand-Prévot faltered, Niewiadoma-Phinney seemed to pull out a level she's never had before in the TT, beating a lot of the riders she hoped to just minimise her losses to. In many ways, I'd call the Polish rider the biggest winner of the day – because she hardly lost anything.

Whilst not in the GC conversation, Lieke Nooijen also hugely impressed with a time that looked like it could even challenge for the win, beaten only by the World Champion Marlen Reusser (Movistar), as she delivered an effort that shows the serious strength and depth in the Visma-Lease a Bike squad.

And some riders performed pretty much exactly as we expected. Sigrid Haugset (Uno-X Mobility) lost the yellow jersey, but will keep memories of her win and day (or in this case half an hour) in yellow forever. Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ) finished third, which was at once good and unremarkable – she gained time on many rivals, but it felt so expected that she would do that that it hardly even felt like a big story. She sits only behind Reusser now, who also did exactly what we were all expecting: smoked the competition to storm to the stage win and take yellow.

Reusser in the driving seat

Reusser said before this race began that she was always underrated as a GC rider, and the fact that she was immediately asked about whether she could try to hold yellow is evidence that the phenomenon is still ongoing. Because really, the answer is quite obviously yes, and if Vollering had gone into yellow, that's probably not the question she would have faced.

But, for one reason or another, Reusser is still underrated, though I'm here to tell you that I think she's in the driving seat of the Tour right now. A lot of teams and riders probably think that they can take time off her in the mountains, but I really wouldn't be so sure.

This is a rider who has finished second overall in both of the other Grand Tours, climbed to seventh on the Colle delle Finestre on a bad day, and has one of the strongest – and most committed – teams around her. As a team Movistar are more than ready to help her through the hard stages, and her climbing ability is immense – anyone counting on her to simply get dropped on Mont Ventoux may be in for a shock.

When my colleagues and I were throwing in our pre-race predictions in Lausanne a few days ago, I gave Marlen Reusser as my winner. I feel only more certain that she's on the right path to win now.

Lidl-Trek are one of the teams that seem to have put the most resources into this TT, bringing in extra staff just for this day, but their two potential GC riders, Isabella Holmgren and Niamh Fisher-Black, lost two and three minutes respectively.

The German team have said they're not necessarily aiming for GC, preferring to race every stage aggressively in search of a stage win, but today's results likely put a dent in any hopes Holmgren and Fisher-Black had of perhaps still surfing into the top 10.

Elisa Longo Borghini had a good result, but the UAE Team L'IMAD rider probably ended the day thinking that it could have been even better, had she not had to stop for a bike change in the final two kilometres. She certainly didn't suffer in the grand scheme of things, and probably had the third-best ride of the GC contenders, but annoyingly it could have been even better.

Fortunately for her, it's a good sign that she's feeling fit, and she's one of the best-placed riders to take advantage of the punchy, Classics-style stages still to come that could actually end up as the key to this GC race.

Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance-Soudal) really struggled, seemingly unable to push the power that she wanted, and she's the biggest mover on GC, slipping from second overall down to 15th at 2:15. Can she ride her way back into the top 10? Probably, but she is now racing from behind.

The Ferrand-Prévot question

A lot of people will probably put Ferrand-Prévot in their list of who suffered today, but I'm not sure it is as simple as that.

Yes, she had a pretty poor TT compared to pretty much all of her rivals but a colleague made the point to me in the press room that maybe we are comparing Ferrand-Prévot to unfair standards. We're contrasting her efforts to the likes of the TT World Champion in what is, literally, her first ITT since returning to the road after a long absence.

Of course, as a GC rider, it was important to look at how she would perform against her main rivals, but to say that she fell shy of any expectations doesn't hold much water because, really, how could we have had any educated expectations?

The other thing is that a deficit of 2:13 actually feels pretty inconsequential when we think about the stages and challenges still to come. Her time loss was, probably, fairly expected in a discipline she hasn't raced properly for years, in a far-from-ideal position as she struggled to get into a more aero set-up, but we actually haven't seen anything to suggest she's not feeling good in general.

We do have evidence that Ferrand-Prévot is missing a little bit of punch and acceleration; she's been saying that since the Classics and it's evident at the Tour too. Still, whilst punch might make the difference in the opening stages, it's not what's going to be important on Ventoux.

That will be about threshold power and sustained efforts, and given Ferrand-Prévot's prowess on the climbs last year, where she gained over three minutes by the end of the race, it doesn't seem unreasonable to think that she could take back 2:13 on that day alone.

This TT was always an unknown for Ferrand-Prévot, her team and us. It's now a known, but that doesn't mean she's done, far from it. The stages the Frenchwoman is able to capitalise on really are still to come, and her time gap to yellow is close enough that it might not be a barrier, but a source of fuel that adds to her fire.

items.title: 'We don't expect that Marlen will explode' – FDJ United-SUEZ focus on keeping up the pressure after Demi Vollering moves into second overall at Tour de France Femmes
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ) may have a strong record in the time trial, having finished third in the discipline at last year's World Championships. However, it seems she was still pleasantly surprised by her performance in the race against the clock on stage 4 of the Tour de France Femmes.

A third place on the stage, trumping all but one of the key overall rivals, also meant moving up to second on the general classification. Plus, given the relatively slim margin to stage winner, world time trial champion Marlen Reusser (Movistar), the gap to yellow is now just 14 seconds.

"Actually, I'm really happy about the TT," Vollering told reporters after the time trial on Tuesday. "I knew that today was really a TT for the TT specialists, for the riders with big power – the big powerhouses – and yeah, I prepared myself mentally that it was possible to lose some time here on riders like Marlen, for example, but that I was so close, it makes me happy."

Just 17.92 seconds separated the two on the stage, with Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike), who is not an overall threat, settling between the pair of riders who have long been high up on the Tour de France Femmes favourites list. What's more, there were some considerable gaps carved out to many other overall rivals.

Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-Oatly) is now the closest rider behind Vollering in the overall standings, at 54 seconds back from Reusser and 40 seconds behind the 2023 race winner. Then, the other pre-race favourites are at least a minute behind yellow, from Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L'IMAD) and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) at 1:03 and 1:09 respectively, while defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike) is 2:13 behind Reusser.

"For me today is one step, a really, really important step, but it's only one step," said team manager Stephen Delcourt.

While Vollering kept the gap to Reusser to a minimum, the French team has always made clear with its words and actions that it's not aiming for anything less than the top step, and right now another rider is occupying it who is going to be hard to dislodge.

"I think Demi made the gap with the other five contenders, but we still have Marlen …and we don't expect that Marlen will explode," said Delcourt.

Plus, even with Ferrand-Prévot having taken a hit in the time trial, she certainly isn't considered out of the running yet, not when – as Delcourt was quick to point out – she put nearly two minutes into her nearest rival, Sarah Gigante (AG Insurance-Soudal), on the Col de la Madeleine last year and gained three minutes on the fourth-placed Vollering.

2025 was an edition in which Vollering had to grapple with an early crash, and she again hit the deck on stage 3 this year, but there was little evidence that she was feeling the impact of this given the performance delivered in the time trial. She was with the physio and doctor after the stage to manage it, said Delcourt.

"We never know the impact of the crash just after, and especially the morning after and especially when she will push for another effort," he said. "I think she's good. She doesn't complain. She was really, really good [in the time trial] but we are really careful, and we are focused. We have only one goal."

That one goal means there is no chance of a let-up for the whole team, which is throwing everything behind the rider who won in 2023 and has finished second in the other three editions.

"For sure we need to gain whatever we can, wherever we can," said Vollering.

items.title: 'We need to change the plan' – Anna van der Breggen's Tour de France Femmes GC hopes thwarted as usual strength exposes weakness
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
The signs had been there in the opening stages of the Tour de France Femmes, but the spotlight of the individual time trial made it painfully clear – Anna van der Breggen may have had the form to fight her way onto the podium of two Grand Tours already this year, though it wasn't holding at the same level for the third.

On stage 1, she had already ceded a little ground to many of her rivals, falling three seconds back from the top group on the punchy finish. However, it would have been simple to retrieve mere seconds if the SD Worx-Protime rider could just replicate the strength of the time trial performance delivered at the Giro d'Italia in June, where she won the race against the clock and in the process carved out a gap of more than a minute to the rest of the field, including world champion Marlen Reusser (Movistar).

However, the outcome two months down the line couldn't have been more different. Instead of the 21 km time trial being the making of the experienced campaigner's overall assault, it was the moment we saw it breaking.

"Anna has already had a couple of days complaining about not having a good feeling, and the time trial is really hard. I mean, you cannot hide, you just need to do it on your own," said SD Worx-Protime sports manager Danny Stam after the stage.

The writing was on the wall for Van der Breggen early, as she went through the 9.7km intermediate time check at 16:08, which already put her 12th at that point even though her key rivals were yet to come. She then finished with a time of 28:39, just enough for 14th place at the end of the day and down 1:09 on stage winner Reusser. Van der Breggen was even behind Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM), a rider who herself was quick to admit the discipline wasn't one of her strengths, and also Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L'IMAD), who had a late mechanical.

Particularly in a peloton that's seen some illness, the obvious question after an uncharacteristic showing in the race against the clock from Gevrey-Chambertin to Dijon was whether or not Van der Breggen was perhaps unwell.

"She doesn't look sick, she doesn't feel sick, her appetite is good," said Stam. "It's just not going how she wants it."

The puzzle remains why, not just for onlookers but also for her team, who have won two stages already with Lorena Wiebes but entered the race with overall hopes too.

"We don't know, we simply don't know," said Stam. "She was good in La Vuelta, she was going good in [the] Giro. Actually, she had a really good altitude camp without any struggles, no sickness, nothing, so it's difficult to understand the body sometimes."

Now, however, the Dutch rider is going to be heading along the path toward the big test on Mont Ventoux already in eighth position overall and with a 1:17 deficit to leader Reusser.

"I think our general ambitions, we need to change the plan on that," said Stam. "So I think further on we focus on the stages, and hopefully Anna also gets some good feeling back in there."

items.title: 'I was maxing out the gears' - Zoe Bäckstedt falls short trying for first Tour de France Femmes stage win
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Zoe Bäckstedt (Canyon-SRAM) admitted that her first appearance at a climbing-heavy Tour de France Femmes would be 'brutal', but her dream of earning a team selection had been accomplished. That was just the beginning of a long checklist that included service as a support rider for 2024 Tour champion Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and flashing the blue and red bands on her Canyon-SRAM jersey as dual British road champion.

"Disappointed," was her reaction to the media after the stage. "I always hope for more in a time trial like this. But yeah, give me maybe an hour or so, and I'll come around to the fact that yeah I got fourth in my first Tour de France time trial."

It wasn't just a matchup of the reigning U23 time trial World Champion against the elite women's World Champion. It was one of the deepest fields of competitors Bäckstedt had ever faced. Multi-time Dutch time trial medalist Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) finished just four seconds behind Reusser for the runner-up spot.

What may have stung the most was getting bumped from the podium by two seconds by former Tour winner Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ). Vollering pulverised the mid-race descent from the time check on the climb of Lacets de Marsannay, gaining five seconds on Reusser to take third on the stage, and in the process knocking the young Briton off the podium.

"I did a super good power for the first half, and then yeah, the second half where we went on the downhill, it was really quick. I was going above 85 [kph], and at that point it's letting the speed do the work," she reflected.

"You can't really do anything extra, you know. Like I was maxing out the gears already, just letting the speed do the work."

She had the third-best intermediate time of the 138 starters, with only Reusser and Nooijen going faster once up the gradual 2km climb averaging 6.7%. In fact, the split time for Reusser was 15:10, with Nooijen 19.5 seconds back and Bäckstedt less than a half-second away from the Dutch woman's time. In the end, only those three riders and Vollering posted times under 28 minutes.

Any questions about adding Bäckstedt to the Canyon-SRAM roster were answered after her double road and TT titles in the British Nationals when she claimed her debut WorldTour road race victory at the Tour de Suisse. She followed the stage 3 win with another podium on stage 4, going second to Reusser.

For good measure, Bäckstedt then won the GC title at the Baloise Ladies Tour for a second consecutive year.

A full week before racing began at the Tour, the British rider confirmed that "time trialling is the one thing that suits me the most. I think it’s [stage 4] going to be my favourite stage of the whole race, and it’s where I want to shine".

Her definition of 'shine' may not have played out as planned, but later assessment should confirm that this fourth was a bright light. And in the process, she took pressure off team leader Niewiadoma for one day, her teammate finishing 13th and moving up two spots in GC to sixth.

items.title: From 'Project Dijon' to 'Project Nice' –New Tour de France Femmes leader Marlen Reusser ready to defend yellow to the end following time trial triumph
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
World time trial champion Marlen Reusser traded her rainbow jersey for a yellow one on stage 4 of the Tour de France Femmes as 'Project Dijon' turned into 'Project Nice'.

The Swiss rider held off a strong challenge from Dutch time trial champion Lieke Nooijen to win by four seconds in France's mustard capital. More importantly, however, she put 17 seconds into Demi Vollering, a minute into Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, and two minutes into defending Tour champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot.

With one of her 'projects' already a success, the next challenge for Reusser and Movistar will be to defend yellow through the Jura and Ardèche, over Mont Ventoux, and all the way to Nice.

"My team is very, very motivated and was very on board for this Project Dijon, how we call it," Reusser told in the post-stage press conference on Tuesday.

"Actually, we never called something 'Project Nice', but I think we have 'Project Nice'. We do everything we can to do that. But, as was the case with 'Project Dijon', you just can't know how everything is going to turn out.

"As I said, I'm super happy that I'm here in yellow. If I stand in Nice in yellow, I'm even happier, but you don't know. We've seen it in so many stage races – so many things can happen; it can change. I'm not at all like, 'I have yellow, I've got to have it in Nice,' but I think it's possible."

Reusser now holds a 14-second advantage over Vollering, while Ferrand-Prévot has a deficit of 2:13 to recoup across the remaining five stages if she's to retain her title. Somewhat ominously, the reigning champion said she was looking forward to the challenge of fighting her way back to the top of the standings.

However, Reusser doesn't expect the Frenchwoman and her Visma-Lease a Bike team to start the attacks in the shorter hills that litter the two upcoming stages to Belleville-en-Beaujolais and Tournon-sur-Rhône.

"Not necessarily Visma is expected to do that, because I think Pauline – I don't know what shape she really is in – her quality last year was on the long climbs, so I would more expect her to try on Mont Ventoux," she said.

"But I don't know what's their plan. These days she didn't look super punchy, so I don't think it's maybe the best stage tomorrow for her, but I'm ready to see what happens."

Reusser's Movistar team appears, on the face of it, a touch underpowered by comparison with those of several rivals, notably Vollering's all-star FDJ United-SUEZ squad. Liane Lippert and Arlenis Sierra figure to be her top lieutenants in the face of the upcoming onslaught.

"Everybody says, 'Now that you're good, what made you change that?' I think I showed already these years that I can climb very fast, but often I had to work in between or in the beginning, and then it's so hard to climb," she said.

"I was like, why should I now, for place seven or five or whatever, kill myself when I have this role? So I was really looking forward to having my leader role, saving my legs, and then trying my best climbing and showing what I can do. That's what we do now."

Reusser's legs will certainly be tested again in the coming days, as, even if Ferrand-Prévot may well hold fire, a host of other, punchier riders, including Vollering, Niewiadoma-Phinney, Elisa Longo Borghini, Paula Blasi, and Anna van der Breggen, all lie within 1:20 of her maillot jaune.

Still, whether she holds the lead for a single day or all the way to the Côte d'Azur, winning her first stage since the final day time trial in Pau three years ago and wearing the famous jersey is certainly reason for celebration.

"This is really special for me because when I was here the first time, I was a domestique, and I really didn't expect that I would win this gravel stage," she said of the first of the trio of Tour stages now headlining her palmarès, in Bar-sur-Aube, only 100km north of Dijon.

"That was a nice thing for me. The time trial, of course, was different, and now it's the first Tour de France that I really had as a big target. I'm really prepared, and I'm here as a leader."

items.title: Despite being 10 years younger than the 'big kids', multi-discipline U23 talent Kylee Hanel thriving in 'long, grueling races of gravel' with Leadville looming
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Just a year ago, while still a teenager, Kylee Hanel was learning the ropes for road racing at kermesses in Belgium and stage races in the US. She proved to be a fast learner.

She competed in competitions at the Tucson Bicycle Classic and the Redlands Bicycle Classic with a club team based near her home in Oregon, showing consistent top-20 results. Then she moved to Aegis Cycling, founded by former USPro road champion Lauren Stephens, for her first UCI races at the Tour of the Gila and the Tour de Bloom, with consistent results on climbing stages and in time trials.

At the one-day Zottegem-Strijpen, Hanel finished in the lead group of six, which was won by Sandrine Tas, who is now with Lotto-Intermarché. She may have been sixth out of the six, but it showed she belonged.

It was in one-day races on home soil, be it dirt or tarmac, that summer where Hanel's name became more familiar to her competitors, as well as future sponsors and racing fans. She finished 10th in the U23 women's road race at USPro Road Nationals, her first appearance at a championships event. Her next championship event was four months later, and she went eighth on the elite stage at US Gravel Nationals.

It's a fast upward trajectory on multiple surfaces for Hanel, but she still speaks with a bit of caution in her voice. She told ahead of her debut at Leadville Trail 100 MTB about her interest in cycling, what she has learned so far and where she would like her career on a bike to lead.

Cyclingnews: Tell us about growing up in Portland, Oregon. How did you get involved in cycling?

Growing up in Portland honestly gave me a lot of opportunities. There's a huge cycling culture here, and even though it's more commuter-style riding, it's still a cycling culture. I grew up going on short rides with my mom Shelley, dad Chris, and sister Caelyn, but when I was 13 I started riding with just my dad. We would do really short rides, like a three-mile ride that would take 25 minutes. But I loved it because I wanted to spend time with him.

For high school, I went to Central Catholic in Northeast Portland, and now I go to Oregon State University, and I'm part of their eCampus program. I am majoring in business with a minor in sports management. I actually decided to do online school because of cycling.

CN: Road racing and some cyclocross in the Pacific Northwest is where you raced the most, but in the past three years you've added gravel racing, so which is your favourite discipline?

If you asked me to choose between gravel and road, I honestly could not tell you which one I prefer more. They are both very different, yet similar. I really like the team aspect of road, but I like the long, gruelling races of gravel.

CN: On the road, you ride now for AEGIS x LOE. How did you connect with her and what have you learned from this experience so far?

I race for Aegis x Leaders of Enchantment right now, and I race under Lauren Stephens. She's definitely a leader, but she's also a teammate. I have learned so much from her. I've not only learned positioning, bike handling skills, and teamwork from her, but the most important thing I learned from her is humility. She knows it's a blessing to be racing and is appreciative of the fact that she gets to go out and race. She doesn't look at the world like it owes her something, which I admire a lot about her.

CN: For gravel, you have a different setup for equipment and your team. Tell us about that.

On the gravel side, I am a privateer. I ride for Cervélo. I got introduced to them through Michael Engleman, who is one of my greatest mentors and my current coach and friend. I didn't have a whole lot of results last year, so Cervélo just saw my power numbers and decided to take a chance on me, which I could not be more grateful for.

Pretty much this year I have just been supported by equipment, which makes sense considering that I really didn't have much of a name for myself until this year. But next year I'm learning about signing contracts where I'll get bonuses and be salaried.

This year Cervélo have provided me with bikes, while PEARL iZUMi is sponsoring me with clothing and shoes, Giro is sponsoring me with helmets, Oakley with glasses, LOOK gave me pedals, Prologo gave me saddles, Reserves and Maxxis are supporting me with tires/wheels.

CN: In 2025 you finished 12th among elite women at SBT GRVL and in the top 10 at US Gravel Nationals, won a third time by Stephens. Did you feel these races proved you were an 'elite' rider off-road?

No, I really didn't feel like an elite road or off-road rider last year. My dad is always telling me that I need to have more confidence in myself, and I am learning that when I line up and race, I have to know that I deserve to be there and that I can win because a lot of cycling is mental. While it was super cool to be racing with what I like to call the "big kids", I would usually assume that if I beat them, it was just because they had a bad race. Now that I'm actually racing with them and performing well alongside them, I still think I view it differently than they view each other, just because I am 10 years younger than most of them. I admire them and look up to them in a way that a middle schooler would look up to somebody in college.

CN: So far in 2026 you've won some big races, including Unbound Gravel 100 and USPro U23 ITT national championship. Tell us what made each of those events special and challenging.

Unbound Gravel 100 and the ITT National Championships were surprisingly similar in terms of mindset. Unbound was such a hard year because of the mud. It was my first year doing it, so I really didn't have any expectations, but from what I've heard from people who have been doing it for two decades, it was a very difficult year. I had to be mentally strong for both. The only difference was that the TT was shorter, and obviously they were on different bikes.

CN: You are at the top of the leaderboard in the women's U23 competition of the Life Time Grand Prix. Which event remaining on the schedule in the LTGP suits you best?

Going into this year, I had no idea and no expectations of what the Life Time Grand Prix U23 was going to be. I have been pleasantly surprised by these events and the amazing people who run them. It is an awesome culture, and I really love being able to race with people who care about racing as much as I do.

I also really like the structure. It's nice because if you have a bad race, you still have other chances to prove that you can perform and be the best. It was an honour to be chosen to be part of the Life Time U23 field, and I hope to race in the elite field next year. The next race that I think will suit me best is probably the last gravel race of the series, Big Sugar. I haven't mountain biked a whole lot, but I started out mountain biking, so I have some high hopes for doing well there, too.

CN: Speaking of mountain biking, next on the calendar in the LTGP series is Leadville Trail 100 MTB. What do you see as most challenging for this event, and what part of the race are you eager to take on?

No, I have not done Leadville yet. This will be my first year. I think the most challenging part of it will be the elevation. I live at sea level, so I'm going two and a half weeks early to train and get used to the elevation, so hopefully there are no major problems while racing. I think I'm most eager to take on this long, seven-plus-hour course because one thing I know about myself is that I persevere.

CN: Living in Oregon, are you able to train with any of the other U23 riders, or elite riders? Who do you tend to train with, or do you just ride solo?

I have become friends with some of the U23 riders in the LTGP series. If I lived in Colorado, I'd probably train with Lauren Aggeler, but we are hours and hours apart. So I train with my friends in Portland, and I train a lot with my dad, who is the one who got me into cycling. I am just now finally able to beat him, haha. However, I do really like to train solo and listen to podcasts and music.

CN: In the next few years, what are the top races you look forward to racing the most? And where would you just like to travel?

I think the race I'm most looking forward to next year is Road Nationals again because I'm always wanting to do better than I did the previous year, and the course stays the same [in Charleston, West Virginia], so it's a good chance for me to see my progress. I also really want to travel to Switzerland and Italy just because of how pretty I've heard the riding is.

CN: Name a few racing goals you would like to achieve this year, and in the coming years.

This year I would really like to do well at the TT and Road World Championships and win the Life Time Grand Prix U23 series. I also really want to place well among the elite LTGP field in the coming years. By the time I am 25, I hope to be living in Europe.

items.title: 'I quite like this scenario of having to go after them rather than being the favourite' – Pauline Ferrand-Prévot down but not out after Tour de France Femmes time trial
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Heading into Tuesday's stage 4 time trial at the Tour de France Femmes, it was expected that defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot would shed time to her GC rivals. A loss of two minutes to stage winner Marlen Reusser and Demi Vollering, last year's runner-up, will sting, though.

On Monday, Visma-Lease a Bike directeur sportif Jos Van Emden told that he was "confident enough" about the Frenchwoman's chances in the 21km ride to Dijon. Now, however, the Dutch squad will be going back to the drawing board as Ferrand-Prévot has to chase a lead, a contrast to last year's coronation in the Alps, where she soared away from everyone on the Col de la Madeleine.

Last Tour's penultimate stage, finishing on the 19km monster, saw Ferrand-Prévot put over two minutes into her main rivals for yellow, and a repeat will now be needed on Mont Ventoux or in the hills of the Jura, Ardèche and Nice either side of the Giant of Provence.

In the aftermath of the stage 4 time trial, held on another sweltering day in Eastern France, Ferrand-Prévot and her team understandably hadn't yet worked out a plan on taking back the Tour.

"Well, there are several possible scenarios. It's true that right now I'm two minutes and 15 seconds behind Marlen," Ferrand-Prévot said.

"On the Madeleine, I managed to make up quite a bit of time. This year, Ventoux is a climb that's going to be long too, so there you go.

"It'll also depend on the others – how they're doing, how much progress they've made. It'll depend on a lot of things, but in any case I'll give it my all to try and claw back that 2:15."

Ventoux may be the day of days in terms of the GC battle. However, the upcoming pair of stages, a 140km ride to Belleville-en-Beaujolais featuring more elevation than Liège-Bastogne-Liège, and a similarly tough 153km ride to Tournon-sur-Rhône, both provide ample opportunity for Ferrand-Prévot and the rest of the contenders to gain time.

The fightback may well start on Wednesday, then, though Van Emden – a leading time trialist in the men's peloton during his racing days – was giving nothing away.

The team was "ready for every time loss," he said, adding that they knew losing such a large amount of time was a possibility during this stage – Ferrand-Prévot's first TT of this length since the French National Championships five years ago.

"Pauline is disappointed that Lieke [Nooijen] missed out on the stage by 4 seconds," was his response to a query about his leader's thoughts on the stage, before he shut down a question on team tactics.

"I have multiple scenarios in my backpack, so looking forward to that. I will never, ever give journalists insight into my thoughts about tactics. Never.

"This year is not last year, but everything is still possible. It could be [tomorrow], or it could be stage 6, stage 7, stage 8, or 9," he concluded with a smile.

Ferrand-Prévot wasn't disappointed by her ride on the day, she said, though she did admit to "feeling a bit silly" about the outcome.

"I gave it my all – it wasn't enough, but there you go," she said.

"I'm proud of having fought as hard as I could, even though I feel a bit silly today about what I managed to achieve. I've got no excuses. I was simply not strong enough, and that's that."

After riding the first stages in more of a defensive role as other punchier riders led the attacking, with Vollering picking up four bonus seconds on the opening day in Lausanne, Ferrand-Prévot and her team might have to switch things up in the coming days.

She said, however, that she's looking forward to the challenge of fighting from behind, though.

"We knew the first three stages were going to be really tough. Yesterday was really intense; it's true that towards the end they attacked and I really struggled to make it to that sprint bonus, so there you go," she said.

"I knew they weren't going to give me any breaks on the short climbs anyway. I know that'll be the case tomorrow too and the days after that, so there you go. Now there's nothing left to do but fight.

"In any case, I quite like this scenario of having to go after them rather than being the favourite myself, so it's going to be a good challenge."

items.title: 'I found my flow' - Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney pulls out one of her best TTs ever to gain on several rivals at Tour de France Femmes
items.content:
It's rare to see a rider as happy as Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) was about finishing 13th in a stage, but the Polish rider couldn't have been more joyful as she returned to her Canyon campervan at their finish in Dijon on Tuesday following the Tour de France Femmes stage 4 time trial.

At the time, Niewiadoma-Phinney didn't even know exactly where she had finished, but she had felt good enough on her time trial bike to be able to celebrate, and did at least know that she had taken time on one big rival, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike).

"It's funny because actually everybody tells me it's good and I haven't seen the results yet," she said at the finish – she finished 13th on the stage, 1:09 down on winner Marlen Reusser (Movistar).

"I felt like I found my flow, I definitely spent a huge amount of time working on my TT skills because as everyone knew, I wasn't the best at it. And yeah, as you can see, if you believe in something and you put a good amount of work in, anything is possible."

What Niewiadoma-Phinney was hoping to be possible was just to limit her losses in the discipline that hasn't always treated her well in the past, but indeed exceeded her own expectations by taking time on some of the riders she seemed sure would finish in front of her.

"The goal for today was to minimise the losses to riders like Demi, Anna van der Breggen, Marlen Reusser, Longo Borghini. It's of course also nice to be in front of Pauline moving towards Mont Ventoux and other harder stages."

So why was Niewiadoma-Phinney so good on Tuesday? She had been careful to not overhype her abilities in the run-up to the TT, but it's also no secret that she's been working on her TT consistently for the last year at least.

"I'm married to a TT specialist, so for once I listened to his advice," she laughed when asked what the key to her improvement was.

"As I said before, I'm very lucky to be surrounded by professional people, in my team looking for details and how to improve my position, Canyon taking me to a wind tunnel, and my coach working on my physical as well as mental side. Also my husband tuning things up and me giving the best today. So I think it's a combination of massive teamwork."

"I'm super grateful to all the people that were with me along the journey to get to this place, because always the Tour de France is such a big goal for myself and my team and we always want to come here to bring that yellow jersey again. Definitely this result puts us closer to the dream," she said.

In the pursuit of that dream, Niewiadoma-Phinney now has perhaps her biggest challenge out of the way, and can look ahead to some still very challenging stages, but ones that suit her abilities more than the race against the clock.

"I was definitely looking forward to this particular moment, to be done with the TT and just focus on the climbs," she said. "Honestly I feel like from tomorrow on, the stage race will properly start.

"Tomorrow it's going to be a super hard stage and we're here to be aggressive. We have a strong team, so we want to do our best. We're in a great shape so what else can you do other than race your bike now?"

items.title: Late mechanical costs Elisa Longo Borghini seconds in strong Tour de France Femmes TT
items.content:
The Italian had to change bikes in the final kilometres, ultimately finishing 1:02 down on winner Marlen Reusser (Movistar) in 10th, but arguably third best of the serious GC contenders, still gaining time on almost all the other overall hopefuls.

She had been flying in the first half of the stage and up the climb, only 21 seconds down on Reusser at the first time check – and faster than Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez) – but needing to change her bike cost her in the second half of the effort.

She was only seven seconds off finishing sixth on the stage.

"Clearly I'm disappointed, because you never want to have a mechanical at two to go, but it is what it is, and you have to accept it," she said at the finish. "I was feeling very well [before the mechanical]."

Despite the bike change, Longo Borghini moved up two spots on GC on Tuesday, now sitting fifth overall, 1:03 down on new yellow jersey Reusser and 49 seconds down on Vollering in second.

Reusser and Demi are the main beneficiaries from the TT, but many other GC contenders are now sitting on fairly similar times, with the effort against the clock significant but not the be-all and end-all of the overall race here.

For Longo Borghini, the disappointment of losing time due to a mechanical was obviously fresh at the finish, but bigger picture, she didn't have many concerns.

"There is still Mont Ventoux, and there are plenty of stages where Pauline [Ferrand-Prevot, who finished 2:12 down] can gain time. I don't think the time trial will be decisive for the GC."

All eyes are of course on Ventoux, but there are plenty more challenges between the TT and the Bald Mountain, and if the first stages are anything to go by, the GC contenders need to be alert every day – which could certainly play to the strengths of the ever-aggressive Longo Borghini.

The Italian wouldn't be drawn on if there were any particular stages or moments she had her eyes on going forward, but did say that "Tomorrow [stage 5] will be an interesting day for sure.

Featuring fewer than nine categorised climbs on the road from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais, stage 5's course has been likened to a World Championships course and will be sure to shake up the overall standings – perhaps even more than today.

On the back foot: defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot suffers major GC setback in Tour de France Femmes time trial
items.content:
In her first competitive individual time trial since 2021, Ferrand-Prévot looked every bit as out of practice as someone who has barely touched their TT bike in years should do.

Even with a climb on the course, the French rider struggled to limit the losses, already 1:21 down on ITT world champion Reusser at the intermediate time check and losing a further 52 seconds before reaching the finish line in Dijon for a gap of 2:13.

While Reusser's victory was tight, just four seconds quicker than Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike), most of the other GC riders were around a minute off the winning time.

That wasn't the case for 2023 race winner and two-time runner-up Demi Vollering, (FDJ United-SUEZ) though, who was the next best big GC name. Vollering finished 17 seconds down on Reusser and so gained 1:55 on Ferrand-Prévot, a huge buffer before the mountains.

Even with the rest of the top climbers losing more than a minute, Ferrand-Prévot's tough day out still means that most of her challengers for the incoming mountains will be starting with a lead over the home star.

Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE L'IMAD) gained 1:10 despite needing a bike change because of a mechanical, with her teammate and 2026 Vuelta Femenina winner Paula Blasi similarly gaining 1:09 over the defending champion.

Kasia Niewiadome-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) also put in a top performance in a discipline that hasn't always been kind to her, gaining 1:04 on Ferrand-Prévot on Tuesday.

Despite not putting in her best performance, Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime) also finished 1:03 up on the Visma rider.

The new GC standings leave last year's yellow jersey 2:13 from the lead, 1:59 off of Vollering, and requiring some serious attacking racing to take back the same title she won a year ago. now behind all of the names she will be looking to defeat on Mont Ventoux and the other key climbs in the coming five stages.

Ferrand-Prévot dropped four places to 15th overall, but can take confidence in the fact that her dominance in the key climbs a year ago saw her win the race by more than 3:40 ahead of Vollering and the rest.

However, she hasn't looked at her best throughout the four stages so far, also missing the front group when racing split up on stage 3, though that move did come back together.

It was clear when the Tour de France Femmes route was announced that this 21km time trial was going to be vital, but the way the events unfolded on Tuesday has changed the whole face of the race.

Reusser can now defend in yellow as she often does excellently, but she will have to do so in the face of a Ferrand-Prévot with nothing to lose and a Vollering in prime striking distance - a scenario which sets up the rest of the week perfectly for fireworks.

items.title: Tour de France Femmes: Marlen Reusser rockets into yellow jersey with victory in Dijon on stage 4 time trial
items.content:
Marlen Reusser (Movistar) won the individual time trial on stage 4 of the Tour de France Femmes, beating Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) by four seconds and Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez) by 18 seconds over a 21km course from Gevrey-Chambertin to Dijon.

With her stage victory, the world ITT champion also takes the yellow jersey for the first time in her career as stage 3 winner and overnight leader Sigrid Ytterhus Haugset (Uno-X Mobility) paid the price for her 88km solo the previous day, losing 3:06 minutes to Reusser and dropping to fourth place overall.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike) had a disappointing day on the TT bike, losing 2:13 minutes to Reusser while Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L'IMAD) and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) could limit their losses to 1:03 minutes and 1:09 minutes, respectively.

Going into the next two hilly stages, Reusser leads the GC by 14 seconds over Vollering, with Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-Oatly) in third place, 54 seconds behind.

"It wasn't perfect perfect, but it was good. I started well, I did a good climb, but I had a little bit of a problem with my bike and the wind. During the recon, it felt a bit different, so I had planned it differently. But in the end, I think I did a good time trial," Reusser could see room for improvement even in her moment of success.

Overall, though, Reusser was overjoyed to see a long-term project come to fruition.

"It's the first Tour de France that was really my goal of the year. We were starting in Switzerland on the Swiss National Day, and on the fourth day, a time trial in Dijon.

"We've been talking about it since Christmas, 'Project Dijon', for the yellow colour of the mustard, to win the time trial and maybe take yellow. It worked out, and I'm really happy," she finished before receiving the yellow leader's jersey on the stage podium.

The 21km ITT course from Gevrey-Chambertin to Dijon started with 8km of flat to rolling roads and then included a climb up the Lacets de Marsannay to the intermediate timing point after 9.7km.

A brief descent and another little uphill took the riders to the highest point of the course after 12km, followed by a fast, almost straight descent into Dijon. Although the forecast rain showers did not materialise, winds from west to southwest provided a tailwind for most of the course, contributing to a fast race.

French ITT champion Célia Le Mouël (Ma Petite Entreprise) was the tenth starter and set a first benchmark with 28:50 minutes, but this was soon beaten by Sandrine Tas (Lotto-Intermarché), who was 0.96 seconds faster, having made up 10 seconds after the timing point.

Tas settled into the hot seat as over 30 riders failed to beat her time, some opting not to go all-out on another hot day in France. Lotte Claes (Fenix-Premier Tech) set a new fastest intermediate time and gained more seconds on the way to the finish, stopping the clock after 28:25 minutes to take the lead.

Nooijen beat Claes' intermediate time by 14 seconds, and on the descent, Nooijen pulled out all the stops, flying down the road and finishing after 27:34 minutes, obliterating Claes' time by 51 seconds.

Zoe Backstedt (Canyon-SRAM), one of the pre-stage favourites, matched Nooijen on the first part of the course and was only 0.29 seconds slower at the timing point, but although the Welsh woman did an excellent second section, she was 16 seconds slower at the finish.

Finally, it was the GC contenders' turn. Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime) could not fulfil expectations, eventually finishing in 14th place and losing time to several of her rivals. White jersey Paula Blasi had been allowed to go all-out by her UAE Team L'IMAD and finished a minute slower than Nooijen. Reusser was almost 20 seconds faster than Nooijen at the intermediate time but lost time on the second part, finishing only four seconds ahead of Nooijen to take the lead.

Ferrand-Prévot struggled on the TT bike, shipping over two minutes to Reusser and more than a minute to Niewiadoma-Phinney and Longo Borghini. The Italian had dropped her chain during the ITT, necessitating a bike change and preventing an even better result. Kerbaol proved her descending skills once again, taking 17 seconds off Niewiadoma-Phinney on the second part of the course to finish in seventh place, 54 seconds behind Reusser.

Vollering had been 23 seconds down on Reusser at the timing point but set the second-fastest time on the second section, only beaten by Nooijen, to take back five seconds and limit her time loss to 18 seconds at the finish.

Haugset finished off the race in the yellow jersey, but her advantage of 2:10 minutes over Reusser was reduced to only five seconds after 9.7km, and the Norwegian eventually finished 3:06 minutes down.

items.title: Vuelta a Burgos: Matthew Brennan wins uphill sprint to Alto del Castillo on opening stage
items.content:
Matthew Brennan (Visma-Lease a Bike) stormed to victory atop the Alto del Castillo on stage 1 of Vuelta a Burgos as the Dutch team dominated the opener, also finishing in second through Ben Tulett on the vicious final ramp.

The British Visma pair had their teammates pace for the majority of the 165-kilometre stage to bring back a four-rider breakaway, which was close – only catching them in the final 2km – but ultimately left them well positioned for the short but steep climb to the line in northern Spain.

Equipo Kern Pharma's Marc Brustenga tried to steal a march with 800 metres of the climb remaining, but quickly ran out of steam and was passed at high-speed by the charging bunch.

Tulett let Brennan into the final 200 metres, where the 20-year-old launched his final sprint, exploding away from his teammate and the rest to his sixth win of the season. Tulett held off Laurence Pithie (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) to confirm the 1-2 for the Dutch team.

The four-rider breakaway that led for most of the opening stage was made up of Josh Burnett (Burgos Burpellet BH), Javier Ibáñez (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA), Valentin Ferron (Cofidis), and Unai Aznar (Euskaltel-Euskadi), attacking 10km into the 165km stage.

Visma-Lease a Bike did most of the work to bring them back, but they were joined by Netcompany Ineos and Lidl-Trek on the front in the final 5km, with the four breakaways still 30 seconds up the road. This gap quickly disappeared in the final 2km, though, allowing the bunch to battle out the uphill sprint for victory.

"Happy, but also quite relieved. I think there's been a lot of hard work, and especially today, the team really showed they believed in me so that was really good to see and I'm really happy it paid off," said Brennan.

"We'll just start with Stevie Kruijswijk, he was out there all alone today, pretty much the whole day, pulling start to finish and then once he was done with a fantastic job keeping the break within distance, the other boys took over and really kept me in a place where I wasn't worried about the guys trying to come around me or anything like that.

"I hit the bottom of the climb in a really good position, and from there all the way up I was still supported – Ben was also there – and then I just had to hit it from the corner. I had a lot of faith in my sprint so I'm really happy it paid off."

The Vuelta a Burgos continues on Wednesday for stage 2, a more tricky climbing day which should be for the GC contenders to Pineda de la Sierra. Brennan should feature again later in the week, as he builds up for the Vuelta a España, where he will race alongside Wout van Aert.

"I'm not sure," he said, when asked what his expectations were for the remaining four stages of the race. "I came here with open ambitions, I didn't quite have the year I've wanted to have, but we went on training camp with all the boys, and we have the Vuelta in mind after this. I think our intentions are to keep to the main goals, try to win where possible, help the guys where possible, and if you can be more successful that's a bonus."

items.title: Tour de Pologne: Jonathan Milan wins fast and furious sprint on stage 2
items.content:
A long, utterly devastating surge of power saw Jonathan Milan (Lidl-Trek) easily fend off the opposition and come through a dangerous late corner perfectly placed for a second straight bunch sprint victory in the Tour de Pologne.

Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) tried hard to anticipate the race leader's last blast for the finish, but after chasing down XDS-Astana's Matteo Malucelli, the Frenchman once again proved powerless to stop the Italian national champion, who was already well ahead.

Given his superiority in the sprint, once a day-long four-rider breakaway had been reeled in, Milan's biggest obstacle was likely getting through a full U-turn corner at 400 metres to go unscathed, upright and well-positioned for the final kick - which he successfully did.

Once Milan opened up his sprint from third place behind Ivan García Cortina (Movistar), Magnier was seemingly in no position to answer, with the Italian doubling up on his stage 1 victory on the second-placed Frenchman, once again by several bike lengths.

"Once again I have to say thanks to my teammates, we managed really well," Milan said later in an audio file provided by his team.

"I was a bit nervous and worried about getting boxed in in the last three kilometres when there were big roads. It was easy to get lost in this kind of washing machine effect. But we always stayed together, the team always pulled for me."

"Those last 450 metres - I was surprised by the gap I got on the guys from Astana. But I had a good start to my sprint and even if it was a super-long one, it went really well."

On a very flat stage with no classified climbs and 91 metres above sea level being the high point of the entire day, the sprinters were always going to be itching for a second straight chance at victory. But neither a spell of brief midday rainfall nor that knowledge of the likely outcome deterred four breakaway riders from making a bid for freedom all the same.

Jonas Rutsch (Lotto-Intermarché), Anton Schiffer (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Polish National Team duo Radoslaw Frątczak and Patryk Stosz were the four who opted to go from distance almost from the gun. However, in a rerun of stage 1's early move, as soon as the break reached around 90 seconds' advantage, Lidl-Trek began tapping out a steady pace behind, evidently to ensure the sprinters in general and Milan in particular wouldn't miss out on such a great opportunity.

Up in the break, the two Poles were the keenest to claim the intermediate sprints that followed, seemingly taking turns to cross the line in first place. Meanwhile the peloton trundled along behind on a series of dense woodland and country roads, waiting for the right moment to light up the pace.

That process began around 65 kilometres to go, as Lidl-Trek and Soudal-QuickStep increased speed steadily and quickly reduced the four riders' gap from 90 to 40 seconds. That didn't stop KoM leader Dries De Bondt (Jayco-AlUla), though, from deciding it was time to bridge across and breathe some more life into the four-rider move.

Not helped by the relentlessly flat terrain along broad A-roads, the Belgian finally made it across after a 15-kilometre pursuit, just as Stosz fell out of the running in the break due to a mechanical. Stosz's teammate Frątczak was still in the thick of it, though, picking up the final intermediate sprint at Goleniów in another short, sharp skirmish.

De Bondt certainly played a critical role in keeping the break alive, taking very long turns on the front on an interminable series of flat highways, as EF, third on Monday with Noah Hobbs behind Milan and Magnier, also showed an interest in chasing behind. Eventually, the combined effort by the sprinters' teams had its near-inevitable effect and finally squeezed all the life out of the break at just under 15 kilometres to go, when observed by vast crowds of holidaymakers, the last of the four ahead were caught.

The series of well-surfaced highways leading to the North Sea coast was ideal for the sprinters' teams to keep things under control in the finale, particularly as NSN and Tudor helped ensure there were no late challengers. The sunshine beat down as the peloton tore across one vast bridge into Szczecin at speeds touching 60 km/h, even if the constantly switching of road-width from four to two lanes and back up again provided perfect conditions for a full-scale washing-machine effect in the bunch.

Netcompany-Ineos made a determined bid for Sam Welsford on the right of the road with three kilometres to go, trying to anticipate the more technical finale. Yet their effort crumpled as Decathlon CGA CMN began bossing the front and the pack swung over another long road bridge and onto a fast but brief section of downhill.

Powering through for Astana on the left-hand side in the final kilometre, Malucelli was perfectly positioned to make it first into the critical U-turn and out the other side. But Milan, too, had made it through the U-turn well-placed and ready to strike, and after a second devastating victory that came just seconds later for the Lidl-Trek star, the odds of Milan taking a third on stage 3's ultra-flat stage are almost equally high.

Manager may have concerns over his group of five central defenders withstanding the demands of a long campaign

Manchester United’s central defender quintet of Leny Yoro, Ayden Heaven, Harry Maguire, Matthijs De Ligt and Lisandro Martínez: an ideal blend of youthful zest and experienced winners or a unit that may prove vulnerable and injury-prone across the long months of the campaign?

In Yoro, Heaven, Maguire, De Ligt, and Martínez, Michael Carrick can talk of high potential and seasoned operators who will patrol the manager’s backline safely. Except it would be understandable if the 45-year-old privately has any concerns about the five defenders, as a unit, especially as there is no plan to strengthen the position unless one (or more) departs.

items.title: Why did Manchester United pay Chelsea £48m for Andrey Santos?
items.author: Ryan Benson
items.content:
Michael Carrick’s first signing is a surprise, but the Brazil midfielder will help the team deal with Casemiro’s exit

Andrey Santos moving from Chelsea to Manchester United was not on our summer transfer window bingo card, but the Brazilian has become Michael Carrick’s first signing. United desperately needed reinforcements in midfield, especially after Casemiro’s departure and Manuel Ugarte’s long-term injury, so deals for Santos and Youri Tielemans will be welcomed by fans.

Tielemans looks like particularly good business – he captains Belgium, has made 244 appearances in the Premier League and was available for £35m – but Santos is a more curious choice. He was often a backup player for Chelsea last season as they finished seven places and 19 points behind United; he is not the finished article, and played for one of United’s rivals. Since Alex Ferguson retired 13 years ago, United had only signed four players from their “big six” rivals: Juan Mata, Nemanja Matic, Mason Mount (all Chelsea) and Alexis Sánchez (Arsenal).
